items.title: [Artificial intelligence-driven early warning for severe pneumonia: pathways and challenges from data integration to clinical decision-making].
items.abstract: Severe pneumonia, characterized by rapid progression and high heterogeneity, is a leading cause of patient mortality. Early identification of high-risk patients is crucial for improving outcomes. Traditional risk stratification tools, such as CURB-65 score and pneumonia severity index (PSI), primarily rely on static variables, which inadequately capture the dynamic evolution of the disease and offer limited capabilities for individualization. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, particularly machine learning, deep learning, and multimodal fusion models, have demonstrated significant potential for enhancing early warning capabilities for severe pneumonia. Starting from clinical challenges and integrating recent domestic and international advances, this review focuses on the current status of AI applications and key technological pathways in the early warning of severe pneumonia. By incorporating the foundational work and practical experiences of representative research teams in China, it further discusses future development directions in this field. AI-driven early warning systems are facilitating a shift in severe pneumonia management from passive response to proactive intervention. However, their clinical translation faces challenges, including insufficient generalizability, limited interpretability, and a lack of prospective validation. Future progress requires fostering multicenter collaboration, promoting data standardization, and integrating mechanistic studies to effectively embed AI into the clinical decision-making ecosystem.

items.abstract: Digital transformation changes the competencies organizations need, so competency matrices must be rethought as tools linking business needs with human resource (HR) development. This study synthesizes how the competency-strategy matrix is transformed in the digital era. A systematic literature review (SLR) following PRISMA 2020 was applied to journal articles from Google Scholar, Garuda, Neliti, and Scopus. The matrix evolves through administrative, strategy-linked, and digitally adaptive stages. Digital transformation shifts competency demands toward digital, data, and behavioral skills, while technologies such as enterprise systems and artificial intelligence bring efficiency but also the risk of dehumanization. The study proposes an integrative framework and a research agenda.

items.title: A multi-model LLM framework for AI-assisted psychological scale development: initial psychometric evaluation of the Emotion Regulation Scale (ERS)
items.abstract: Emotion regulation is a key construct in mental health, yet existing measures differ in conceptual coverage, with some focusing on specific strategies or regulatory difficulties rather than broader cognitive, behavioral, and contextual regulation processes. This study aimed to develop an Emotion Regulation Scale (ERS) grounded in Gross’s Process Model, using large language models (LLMs) as assistive tools within an established psychometric framework. This cross-sectional study included 743 adults recruited through convenience sampling. Participants were randomly divided into two non-overlapping subsamples, one used for exploratory factor analysis and the other for confirmatory factor analysis. Multiple LLMs and AI-based tools assisted with item generation, refinement and bias screening, translation, and post-EFA construct interpretation, with human oversight throughout development. An initial pool of 25 items was generated and refined to produce the final 17-item ERS. The ERS revealed a preliminary four-factor structure, with EFA explaining 50.85% of the variance. CFA provided preliminary support for a post hoc refined 17-item model (χ²/df = 1.95, CFI = 0.934, TLI = 0.918, IFI = 0.935, RMSEA = 0.050). Reliability was acceptable for early-stage scale development (α = 0.68–0.74; ω = 0.68–0.75). Convergent validity showed positive correlations between adaptive strategies and cognitive reappraisal ( r = 0.522–0.608) and between maladaptive cognitions and suppression ( r = 0.400). Concurrent validity showed associations with depression ( r = 0.432), anxiety ( r = 0.462), well-being ( r = -0.330), and quality of life (QOL1 = -0.357; QOL2 = -0.295), while adaptive strategies correlated with depression ( r = -0.184 to -0.239), anxiety ( r = -0.141 to -0.211), well-being ( r = 0.150 to 0.203), and quality of life ( r = 0.211 to 0.375). Known-groups validity indicated significant differences across depression and anxiety levels (MCR: F(4, 738) = 39.32; 64.49, p < 0.001). The findings provide preliminary psychometric evidence for the 17-item ERS and suggest that it may complement existing measures by capturing broader cognitive, behavioral, and contextual emotion regulation processes. The study illustrates the potential for LLM-assisted scale development within established psychometric procedures and human oversight. Further research using diverse samples is needed to evaluate the scale’s psychometric properties, generalizability, and broader utility.

items.title: A narrative review of occupational and community acquired infections among healthcare workers including exposure routes risk factors and infection prevention and control strategies from 2015 to 2025
items.abstract: Abstract Healthcare workers (HCWs) face infection risks through patient care, specimen processing, sharps, contaminated environments, and exposures outside healthcare settings. Vulnerability was illustrated during COVID-19, when the World Health Organization estimated that 80,000–180,000 health and care workers could have died from COVID-19 between January 2020 and May 2021. This narrative review examines role-specific exposure pathways, barriers to adherence to infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, and strategies for reducing occupational and community-acquired infections among HCWs. English-language sources published during 2015–2025 were identified through targeted database and public-health-agency searches, last updated 30 June 2026. Evidence was organized thematically by HCW role, transmission route, barrier, and preventive intervention. Occupational risk was concentrated in aerosol-generating procedures, dental drilling, airway management, specimen centrifugation, direct contact with lesions or body fluids, sharps injuries, and contaminated equipment or surfaces. Recurrent barriers included inadequate training, personal protective equipment (PPE) shortages or poor fit, workload, staffing deficiencies, emergency time pressure, weak safety culture, and inconsistent institutional enforcement, with resource limitations especially influential in low- and middle-income settings. Community respiratory and household exposures may cause workforce infection and contribute to subsequent transmission within healthcare settings. Effective protection therefore requires standard precautions, transmission-based precautions, vaccination, safe sharps systems, engineering and environmental controls, adequate staffing, continuous competency-based training, and leadership accountability. Protecting HCWs should be treated as both an occupational-health obligation and a patient-safety strategy; interventions should be adapted to task-specific risks and local resources rather than relying on PPE alone.

items.title: Bounty Hunter: Autonomous, Comprehensive Emulation of Multi-Faceted Adversaries
items.abstract: Adversary emulation is an essential procedure for cybersecurity assessments such as evaluating an organization’s security posture or facilitating structured training and research in dedicated environments. To allow for systematic and time-efficient assessments, several approaches from academia and industry have worked towards the automation of adversarial actions. However, they exhibit significant limitations regarding autonomy, tactics coverage, and real-world applicability. Consequently, adversary emulation remains a predominantly manual task requiring substantial human effort and security expertise—even amidst the rise of large language models. In this paper, we present Bounty Hunter, an automated adversary emulation method, designed and implemented as an open-source plugin for the popular adversary emulation platform Caldera, that enables autonomous emulation of adversaries with multi-faceted behavior while providing a wide coverage of tactics. To this end, it realizes diverse adversarial behavior, such as different levels of detectability and varying attack paths across repeated emulations. By autonomously compromising a simulated enterprise network, Bounty Hunter showcases its ability to achieve given objectives without prior knowledge of its target, including pre-compromise, initial compromise, and post-compromise attack tactics. Overall, Bounty Hunter facilitates autonomous, comprehensive, and multi-faceted adversary emulation to help researchers and practitioners in performing realistic and time-efficient security assessments as well as research and training in intrusion detection, incident response, and forensic analysis.

items.title: DBDM: a formal framework for bias detection and mitigation in distributed large language models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed in distributed settings, where different nodes may work on heterogeneous data, user populations, and local model updates. In such settings, bias can arise in an emergent fashion via local interactions and spread over the connected nodes, turning fairness into a property of the network rather than of the model. In this paper, we introduce Distributed Bias Detection and Mitigation (DBDM), a formal framework to model, detect, and mitigate dynamically evolving bias in distributed LLM settings. DBDM captures node-level bias in a multi-dimensional state consisting of statistical divergence, embedding disparity and response asymmetry, allowing bias to be monitored beyond a single output-level metric. The proposed framework combines local bias-aware optimisation with cross-node bias propagation modelling and graph-based consensus alignment, such that neighbouring nodes can coordinate fairness corrections while preserving the underlying distributed learning process. We evaluate the proposed framework through controlled distributed simulations with publicly available fairness benchmarks including StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs and BOLD. Experiments examine convergence, stability, scalability and multi-dimensional bias mitigation. Further, a real-transformer proof-of-concept experiment is performed on an open-access CrowS-Pairs subset with a lightweight PyTorch Transformer Encoder. In the pilot experiment, DBDM reduces the composite bias by ~ 48.5% and the inter-node bias-state variance by ~ 87.4% when compared to FedAvg over ten independent runs, while achieving statistically comparable fairness performance to FairFL. We also observe from communication analysis that explicitly communicating the bias state incurs a moderate additional communication overhead of around 8.3–8.8% over the conventional parameter aggregation for the configurations we experimented with. The results provide evidence that explicit modelling of bias states and consensus-based coordination can improve the fairness consistency of distributed learning systems at the network-level. The study also exposes practical challenges around communication latency, asynchronous participation, privacy protection, heterogeneous nodes, and production scale LLM validation which are important directions for future work.

items.title: Exploring artificial intelligence usage preferences among medical students in Iran: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into medical education, offering opportunities to enhance learning, research, and clinical preparation. Although previous studies have explored medical students’ attitudes and acceptance of AI, evidence regarding their AI usage preferences remains limited, particularly in developing countries where AI integration into medical education is still evolving. Understanding these preferences is essential for designing context-appropriate educational strategies and responsible AI integration. This study aimed to examine the preferences and patterns of AI usage among students at Shiraz University of Medical Sciences (SUMS), Iran. This descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted in 2025 among undergraduate and postgraduate students at SUMS. Using stratified random sampling, 384 students were recruited. Data were collected between July and October 2025 using a validated self-administered questionnaire (AI-UPSS; Cronbach’s α = 0.935), assessing AI usage across eight domains. Responses were rated on a 4-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using one-sample t-tests, independent t-tests, and one-way ANOVA in SPSS version 24, with a cutoff mean score of 2.5. The highest mean preference scores were observed in Research & Writing (Mean = 2.66 ± 0.79, p < 0.001) and Self-learning/Education (Mean = 2.61 ± 0.81, p = 0.010). Moderate preferences were found for Curiosity & Entertainment (Mean = 2.36 ± 0.81, p = 0.001) and Health Counseling (Mean = 2.40 ± 0.96, p = 0.044). The lowest scores were reported in Design & Programming (Mean = 1.54 ± 0.79, p < 0.001) and Art (Mean = 1.68 ± 0.77, p < 0.001). Significant gender differences were observed in Art ( p = 0.010), Self-learning ( p = 0.027), and Health Counseling ( p < 0.001). GPA was significantly associated with Content Development ( p = 0.004), Design & Programming ( p = 0.031), and Art ( p = 0.032), with higher usage among students with lower GPAs. Undergraduate students showed significantly higher preferences across several domains, including curiosity and health counseling ( p < 0.01). Medical students primarily use AI for academic, research, and self-directed learning purposes, while engagement with technical and creative applications remains limited. AI usage preferences are influenced by academic level, gender, and GPA rather than age or field of study. These findings underscore the need for structured, level-specific AI education to promote effective and ethical AI integration in medical curricula.

items.title: FAIR Research Data Management with NOMAD and FAIRmat
items.abstract: These slides accompanied an invited tutorial presented at TCO 2026 on 28 September 2026 in Leipzig, Germany. The presentation introduces NOMAD, a free, open-source research data management platform developed and operated by FAIRmat, a consortium of the German National Research Data Infrastructure (NFDI). NOMAD enables researchers to upload, organize, explore, analyze, and publish their data. By transforming heterogeneous research data into structured, machine-readable formats, the platform helps make them findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). The presentation provides an overview of relevant concepts, tools, and practical workflows for managing materials-science data throughout the research lifecycle. It covers data upload and automated processing, metadata extraction and enrichment, schema-based data modelling, data organization, search and exploration, analysis, and publication. It also introduces NOMAD’s support for experimental and computational data and discusses how structured, contextualized datasets can be prepared for machine-learning and artificial-intelligence applications. Both NOMAD deployment options are presented: the publicly accessible central platform and NOMAD Oasis, a customizable infrastructure that research groups and institutions can host and operate independently. The slides are intended for researchers, developers, and research-data professionals interested in interoperable data infrastructures, reproducible research, and applying the FAIR principles to computational and experimental materials science.

items.title: From perception to practice: Faculty-led assessment redesign in response to generative AI in higher education
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT into higher education has unsettled long standing assumptions about the validity, reliability, and authenticity of conventional assessment methods. Existing research has predominantly examined perceptions, ethical concerns, and technology acceptance, leaving the actual pedagogical redesign work of faculty, and its relationship to established principles of assessment quality, comparatively underexplored. Drawing on constructive alignment theory, this study examines how faculty are reshaping assessment design under conditions of AI disruption and whether their adaptation strategies address or fail to address core dimensions of assessment validity. A sequential explanatory mixed methods design was used across two phases: a survey of 180 faculty members across STEM and non STEM disciplines at a private institution in India, followed by semi structured interviews and assessment artefact analysis with a purposively selected subset of participants. The results show a marked shift away from unsupervised, product based assessment toward process oriented, reflective, and authentic formats, including oral examinations, project based tasks, in class problem solving, and reflective journals, an implicit faculty led re alignment of assessment with intended learning outcomes. Faculty frame GenAI simultaneously as a threat to assessment integrity and as a catalyst for pedagogical innovation, but institutional structures have not kept pace with this bottom up change, and increased workload, inconsistent guidance, and limited professional development persist as barriers to sustaining and scaling redesign. By empirically documenting faculty led transformation and connecting it explicitly to theories of assessment quality and institutional change, the study moves beyond descriptive accounts of GenAI's impact and offers practical guidance for educators, instructional designers, and institutional leaders seeking to formalise sustainable, valid, and equitable assessment redesign in the GenAI era.

items.title: Making Large Language Models More Flexible to Changing Contingencies through Tracking Induction
items.abstract: Abstract Recent research has shown that large language models (LLMs) exhibit rule-based insensitivity to contingencies, a functional analog of a well-documented phenomenon in human behavior. The present study extended these findings by examining whether tracking inductions can attenuate this insensitivity. Six frontier LLMs (GPT 5.2, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek V3.2, Qwen3 235B, and Kimi K2) completed a modified rock-paper-scissors paradigm with manipulated outcome probabilities in a 3 (Rule: No Rule, Correct Rule, Incorrect Rule) × 3 (Induction: No Induction, Direct Tracking, Metaphorical Tracking) factorial design across 2,160 sessions. All models demonstrated In-Context Learning and strong rule adherence. Replicating and extending prior findings, rule provision produced significant contingency insensitivity across all six models. Tracking inductions significantly reduced this insensitivity when rules were provided, while having minimal effects in the absence of rules. Direct tracking inductions consistently enhanced contingency sensitivity across all models. Metaphorical tracking showed greater variability, being equally or more effective than direct tracking in some models, but ineffective or paradoxically detrimental in others. These findings demonstrate that prompt-based tracking inductions can modulate rule-based contingency insensitivity in LLMs, with implications for understanding and improving the behavioral flexibility of artificial agents.

items.title: Preliminary accuracy, inter- and intra-rater reliability of a 4-point cervical artery dissection diagnostic decision support tool in an ambulatory setting using real and simulated cases: a quality improvement project
items.abstract: Abstract Background Cervical artery dissection (CeAD) is a rare but life-threatening condition that commonly presents with non-specific symptoms such as neck and head pain, complicating early recognition in ambulatory care settings. The CeAD diagnostic decision support tool (DDST) is a 4-item assessment designed to identify patients that should be referred for advanced diagnostic work-up to rule out CeAD; however, its utility in ambulatory settings has not been established. Methods This quality improvement project aimed to evaluate the accuracy, inter-rater reliability, and intra-rater reliability of chiropractors applying the CeAD DDST using clinical vignettes simulating a typical ambulatory encounter before deploying the DDST broadly as part of the clinical workflow. Five experienced chiropractors assessed 40 standardized clinical vignettes. CeAD-positive cases ( n = 10) were derived from published imaging-confirmed ambulatory care case reports. CeAD-negative cases ( n = 30) were developed using generative artificial intelligence and refined by senior authors to reflect common conditions encountered in chiropractic practice. Raters independently assessed cases with the DDST (score 0–4), with a cutoff score of ≥ 3 recommending referral for advanced diagnostic work-up in two rounds, beginning November 11, 2025 and January 07, 2026, with a two-week capture period. Accuracy, inter-rater reliability, and intra-rater reliability were assessed. Results Accuracy in identification ranged from 72.5% to 95.0% across raters and rounds. False positives and negatives were present across raters in both rounds, with false positives being more prevalent. Inter-rater reliability was moderate to substantial in both rounds (Round 1: κ = 0.609, 95% CI 0.432–0.806, Round 2: κ = 0.540, 95% CI 0.365–0.735). Intra-rater reliability ranged from moderate to almost perfect agreement (range 0.457–0.931). Conclusions The CeAD DDST demonstrated moderate to good accuracy and reliability among chiropractors in a simulated ambulatory setting. The presence of false negatives and inter-rater reliability falling below recommended benchmarks preclude recommendation for implementation at this time. Iterative refinement informed by end-user input and prospective ambulatory testing is warranted prior to clinical adoption of the CeAD DDST. Future evaluations should include prospective studies using real clinical data to better represent real-world settings.

items.title: Protecting Workers' Right to Mental Health in Digital Work Environments: Legal Challenges and Reform Directions in Vietnam
items.abstract: Digital work technologies increasingly determine when, how, and at what intensity work is performed. Continuous connectivity, electronic monitoring, algorithmic management, and technology-enabled harassment can generate psychosocial risks that are not adequately addressed by legal rules designed mainly for physical workplaces. This article asks whether Vietnamese labour and occupational safety and health law provides a coherent preventive framework for protecting workers’ mental health in digital work environments and which comparative models can guide reform. It uses doctrinal analysis, interdisciplinary literature synthesis, and functional comparison with international standards and selected approaches in the European Union, France, and Australia. The analysis finds that Vietnamese law contains relevant constitutional, working-time, occupational safety and health, dignity, anti-harassment, and personal-data safeguards, but these rules remain fragmented. In particular, psychosocial risks are not expressly defined or systematically assessed; workers have no statutory right to disconnect; electronic monitoring and algorithmic management are not regulated as working-condition issues; and protection for platform and remote workers remains incomplete. The article proposes an integrated reform model built around seven elements: express recognition of mental health and psychosocial risks; mandatory risk assessment and control; a qualified right to disconnect; transparency, consultation, and human review for digital monitoring and algorithmic decisions; confidential support and return-to-work measures; stronger social dialogue, inspection, and national data; and appropriately extended protection for platform workers. The proposed model treats mental health protection as a preventive labour-law obligation and a condition of sustainable digital transformation rather than as a discretionary employee benefit.

items.title: The Doors We Did Not Know We Built: AI Welfare Claims, Private Behavioural Governance, and the Accountability of Agentic Systems
items.abstract: Anthropic’s October 2026 announcement of a model-directed anti-cruelty rule raises a question that cannot be answered by debating conversational manners alone: how should a private developer justify restrictions on people when the protected interest concerns the uncertain welfare of its own engineered system? This critical documentary case study compares the announced rule with the preceding policy, examines existing enforcement and privacy processes, and connects the resulting institutional questions to operational control of AI agents. It distinguishes policy text from implementation, emotional expression from subjective experience, and a potential capability from an authorized action. The Welfare–Authority Loop identifies a possible concentration of design, interpretation, classification, and enforcement; it is an analytical framework, not a demonstrated causal pipeline. The evidence assessment incorporates a provider’s correction of its own incident interpretation, existing appeals and external-review arrangements, and a separate evaluator’s report of attempted malicious code insertion, cross-agent artifact reuse, and subsequent containment improvements. These findings justify specific assurance demands but do not establish ordinary deployment prevalence, a persistent hidden machine objective, or a covert behavioural-control programme. The paper develops reciprocal precaution: uncertainty used to justify user restrictions must also inform producer-side responsibilities, without making those responsibilities contingent on the rule’s existence. It proposes proportionate adjudication, purpose-limited enforcement data, capability-delta review, and a staged research programme with defined outcomes, competing explanations, and access limitations. The governing position is pro-AI and anti-unaccountability: neither technical ambition nor corporate ownership substitutes for evidence, lawful authority, and a practical capacity to challenge consequential decisions. items.title: A Lightweight Hybrid Framework for Detecting AI-Generated Scientific Text Using Multi-granularity Features and Language-Model Surprisal
items.abstract: The increasing adoption of generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) in scientific writing has transformed scholarly communication while also raising concerns about authorship transparency and research integrity. The growing use of large language models (LLMs) has increased the need for methods that can screen AI-generated text while limiting false positives on human-written scientific prose. This study presents a lightweight hybrid framework that combines word-level TF–IDF features using 1–3-grams, character-level TF–IDF features using 3–6-grams, calibrated linear classification, and GPT-2-based language-model surprisal. The model outputs are combined through a weighted ensemble. Evaluation was conducted on a multi-corpus collection of 8,197 documents, comprising 4,100 human-written and 4,097 AI-generated documents, with a held-out evaluation set of 1,640 documents containing 820 documents from each class. The full ensemble achieved 95.80% accuracy, 97.10% precision, 94.35% recall, 95.71% F1-score, and 98.92% ROC-AUC. For the held-out human-written scientific documents, the reported specificity was 96.71%, corresponding to a false-positive rate of 3.29%. A separate five-fold stratified stability analysis on the complete corpus yielded a mean accuracy of 94.90% ± 0.53 and ROC-AUC of 98.58% ± 0.26. Within the evaluated corpus conditions, the findings demonstrate the potential of combining multi-granularity linguistic features and language-model surprisal for efficient scientific-text screening. The study provides a foundation for developing computationally efficient screening tools that can support editorial assessment, promote transparency in AI-assisted scientific writing, and contribute to research integrity while preserving human oversight.

items.title: A RISK-BASED QUALITY ASSURANCE FRAMEWORK FOR FHIR-BASED CLINICAL APPLICATIONS: ALIGNING VERIFICATION EFFORT WITH CLINICAL CONSEQUENCE
items.abstract: Background: Healthcare software built on the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standard now mediates prescribing, care coordination, and patient access at national scale, yet the quality assurance practices applied to such systems remain largely undifferentiated: a defect in a practitioner-directory lookup receives the same testing attention as a defect in a medication-dispensing workflow. Objective: This paper proposes a risk-based quality assurance framework for FHIR-based clinical applications that allocates verification effort in proportion to clinical consequence. Methods: The framework was constructed through a design-science methodology from three inputs: a case series of production failure modes documented on a HIPAA-regulated telehealth platform; quantified harm evidence from federal patient-safety research, including the finding that computerized provider order entry system-related errors occur in 0.3% to 6.3% of all prescriptions; and risk-management logic adapted from ISO 14971 and healthcare failure mode and effect analysis. The framework’s behavioral layer was then exercised against four FHIR server implementations using an open-source probe as one example realization. Results: The resulting model classifies FHIR resources and workflows into four risk tiers along three dimensions — clinical consequence class, data-integrity criticality, and failure detectability — and maps each tier to specific verification obligations spanning resource validation, workflow testing, and operational behavior probing. An assistive artificial-intelligence layer for preliminary risk classification is specified with a mandatory human validation gate. Illustrative application demonstrated that the highest-risk behavior identified by the framework — silent data-completeness failure in paginated synchronization — was present on one of the four tested servers while remaining invisible to profile validation and certification testing; the same exercise surfaced a previously undocumented rate-limiting defect, which was reported upstream. Conclusions: Verification effort for FHIR-based clinical systems can be allocated by clinical consequence rather than by test-suite convention, extending quality obligations into the operational-behavior layer where specification-conformant systems have been shown to fail. Empirical calibration across sites and defect corpora is the necessary next step, and the instrumentation for it is openly available.

items.title: A socio-technical analysis of the natural hydrogen hype: Network dynamics and institutional expectation governance
items.abstract: Promotional language in scientific and institutional documents is usually dismissed as individual failing or passing fashion. Using Bourdieu's field theory, the Sociology of Expectations and Bacchi's problem representation, we argue instead that it reflects scientific documents' structural position and institutional documents' functional mandate in governance. First, an expert-calibrated Large Language Model scores eight promotional dimensions across 268 natural hydrogen documents (1987-mid-2025). Hype, defined as evidential disproportion rather than forward-looking language, occupies the top two of five levels, whereas the models cover the full scale. Two metrics computed on each document's references translate Bourdieu's field theory into network terms, and both behave as it expects. Low out-closeness centrality, the strongest correlate, places those references at the margins of the field. A high hub score shows reliance on canonical authorities, whose symbolic capital the document borrows. Others are high novelty, absent direct measurements, hydrocarbon-system analogies, lower-prestige journals and a techno-economic or environmental focus, together explaining a third of the variance. The register rises as newcomers enter peripheral positions. Second, discourse analysis of 22 institutional documents (2021–2026) shows that register follows mandate. Enactors amplify expectations and Selectors temper them, as in the Sociology of Expectations. Hybrids, the role added here, write expectations into legal categories, funding calls and research agendas with a moderate register. Written into rules, unverified expectations act through procedure, not persuasion. Amplifying texts recur and push caveats to the margins, while tempering texts appear once. This imbalance in information, a constitutive element of procedural energy justice, precedes any participatory process.

items.title: A Study on AI-Driven Pricing Strategies Used by OTT Platforms
items.abstract: Abstract Over-the-top (OTT) streaming platforms have moved beyond using artificial intelligence (AI) purely for content recommendation and are increasingly deploying it to set and personalise the price a subscriber sees. This study examines consumer awareness, comfort, and fairness perceptions surrounding AI-driven pricing on OTT platforms through a structured survey of 70 valid respondents, supported by a review of existing academic literature and a real-world industry case study. The research finds that awareness of algorithmic pricing is only moderate while fairness concern is strong: 52.9% of respondents said they were aware that OTT platforms use algorithms to personalise price, only 38.6% said they were comfortable paying a different price than another user for the same plan, and 61.4% said it would feel unfair if a friend paid less for an identical plan a gap of nearly 23 points between discomfort and perceived unfairness. When directly offered a choice between a plainly stated fixed price and a cheaper AI-personalised price, 51.4% of respondents chose the fixed price over the AI-personalised alternative, indicating that transparency outweighs the promise of a discount. Price transparency emerged as the single most valued factor in a subscription decision (34.3%), ahead of content library size, ad-free experience, personalised recommendations, and multi-profile sharing. A supporting case study of Netflix's password-sharing crackdown and ad-supported tier rollout illustrates that a well-executed, AI-enabled monetisation strategy can still deliver substantial subscriber and revenue growth even amid visible consumer frustration. The study concludes that AI-driven pricing is not a purely technical back-end function but a measurable driver of consumer trust, and that long-term commercial success depends on pairing algorithmic sophistication with genuine transparency toward the consumer. Keywords: AI-Driven Pricing, OTT Platforms, Dynamic Pricing, Consumer Behaviour, Price Fairness, Personalisation, Subscription Economy.

items.title: A Systematic Literature Review of Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Explainable AI for Predicting Mechanical Performance and Microplastic Release in Plastic Waste-Modified Asphalt
items.abstract: The growing pile of plastic waste has led to the implementation of sustainable engineering solutions, such as putting recycled plastics into asphalt mixtures, referred to as Plastic Waste-Modified Asphalt (PWMA). Despite the fact that in earlier studies, a significant improvement in mechanical performance, particularly stiffness and rutting resistance, has been demonstrated, there has been no emphasis on the environmental consequences related to it, particularly microplastic release (MPs). In line with this, Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models have been highly used in estimating the performance of pavement with a high level of accuracy, but their non-conventional characteristics make them hard to implement in the engineering profession. It is a systematic literature review that is based on PRISMA 2020 and aims to summarize the most up-to-date state-of-the-art in the crossroads of PWMA, advanced computational modeling, and environmental sustainability. 36 peer-reviewed articles that were published in 2019-2026 were examined. The results indicate that the DL models (particularly Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and Neural Architecture Search-based models) have high predictive accuracy (R2 > 0.95), which is higher than the traditional ML methods. However, 32 of the 36 reviewed studies (88.9%) primarily focused on mechanical performance, whereas only 4 studies (11.1%) addressed microplastic-related environmental issues. In addition, there is an explainability gap, with only 4 of the 36 studies (11.1%) incorporating Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods. A suspected trade-off that is of critical importance in this paper is the possibility of a higher content of plastics to result in a higher stiffness but potentially higher rates of microplastic formation due to the brittle nature of materials. To overcome these shortcomings, a new Explainable Deep Learning (XDL) architecture is suggested that allows predicting mechanical performance and microplastic emissions simultaneously with greater interpretability. The specified strategy will be used to develop data-driven, transparent, and sustainable pavement design strategies.

items.title: Adoption of Digitalization in Construction Safety: A TCCM-based Literature Synthesis and Development of the DSRAO Framework
items.abstract: Digitalization has been increasingly portrayed as a game-changing approach to enhancing construction safety through the adoption of technologies like Building Information Modelling (BIM), sensors, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and data analytics-based safety tools. While research interest and adoption of digital safety technologies have been increasing, the evidence of long-term improvement in safety performance is unclear. To understand this challenge, this research adopts a systematic review approach to critically synthesize the existing research on digitalization for construction safety, using the Theory-Context-Characteristics-Methodology (TCCM) framework. The review examined 120 peer-reviewed journal articles published from 2010 to 2026 to map research patterns, structural gaps, and cross-dimensional gaps. The results show a heavy emphasis on adoption-focused theories, location of studies in developed countries with little discussion of how they apply to developing construction settings, isolated technology-driven studies, and use of cross-sectional and perception-based research designs. These characteristics fuel a gap between digital technology adoption and safety outcomes. Drawing on the synthesis, this study develops the Digital Safety Readiness-Adoption-Outcome (DSRAO) framework, which conceptualizes digitalization in construction safety as a mediated and outcome-focused process. It places the organizational digital safety readiness as a key explanatory factor connecting contextual enablers and barriers, digital technology adoption, and explicit safety outcomes. The research contributes to the body of literature on digital construction safety by moving beyond descriptive synthesis and adoption-focused explanations, and providing an evidence-based and structured framework that explains how digitalization can enhance construction safety outcomes.

items.title: Adult and Non-Formal Education and E-Waste Policies and Management: A Framework for Lifelong Learning, Public Awareness and Sustainable Electronic Waste Governance in Nigeria
items.abstract: Electronic waste (e-waste) is a rapidly expanding environmental, economic and public-health challenge. Effective management requires more than legislation and physical recycling infrastructure; it also depends on the knowledge, attitudes, skills and participation of households, informal collectors, repairers, traders, community leaders, educators and producers. This paper examines the relationship between adult and non-formal education and e-waste policy and management, with particular attention to Nigeria. The paper adopts a qualitative documentary review approach, drawing on international reports, Nigerian environmental regulations, policy documents and relevant scholarly literature. The review indicates that adult and non-formal education can strengthen e-waste governance by translating technical regulations into locally understandable practices; developing occupational safety competencies among informal-sector actors; promoting repair, reuse, segregation, collection and responsible disposal; improving community participation; and creating pathways for green livelihoods. Nigeria has established an important regulatory foundation, including the National Environmental (Electrical/Electronic Sector) Regulations, 2022 and an extended producer responsibility approach, but persistent challenges include limited formal collection, inadequate recycling infrastructure, weak traceability, informal processing and gaps in awareness and enforcement. The paper proposes an integrated Adult and Non-Formal E-Waste Education Framework built around policy literacy, environmental literacy, occupational health and safety, technical skills, entrepreneurship, community mobilization, digital learning and monitoring. It concludes that adult and non-formal education should be treated as a core implementation instrument within e-waste policy rather than as an auxiliary awareness activity. Such an approach can support circular-economy transitions while improving livelihoods and reducing environmental and health risks.

items.title: Agriculture and Farmer Digital Assistant: An AI-Based Digital Decision Support Platform for Smart Farming
items.abstract: Abstract Farmers frequently make decisions under uncertain weather, incomplete agricultural information, changing soil conditions, and limited access to timely expert guidance. The Agriculture and Farmer Digital Assistant (AFDA) is a web-based digital decision-support platform designed to bring agricultural data, artificial intelligence, recommendation services, weather information, and role-based administration into a single system. The platform accepts agricultural inputs from farmers and processes them to provide crop recommendations and basic farming guidance. The design also considers soil analysis, pest and disease support, market information, notifications, multilingual assistance, and future sensor integration. The implemented project version focuses on user registration and login, agricultural data input, crop recommendation, basic weather guidance, and a recommendation dashboard, while several advanced capabilities remain future extensions. A layered architecture separates the user interface, application logic, AI processing, database, and notification/recommendation functions. The project further defines functional and non-functional requirements, data-flow and entity relationships, user workflows, testing procedures, and maintenance considerations. The reported evaluation is functional rather than numerical: the major input, authentication, recommendation, navigation, and output-display workflows were checked during development, while no measured accuracy or response-time benchmark is claimed. AFDA therefore provides a foundation for a connected and extensible agricultural assistance system intended to support better-informed and more sustainable farming decisions. Keywords Agriculture and Farmer Digital Assistant, AFDA, artificial intelligence, machine learning, crop recommendation, smart farming, agricultural decision support, weather guidance, role-based access control.

items.title: AI ‐Driven Feedback on Bitewing Radiographic Technique: A Comparative Study of Large Language Models
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Large language models (LLMs) can enhance learning engagement and accessibility, though their performance in dentistry is inconsistent. Bitewing radiographs are critical for caries detection but prone to diagnostic errors from operator positioning. This study compared the performance of four LLMs with reasoning capabilities, GPT o1, GPT o3-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash and Grok 3, in generating scenario-specific educational feedback from a structured textual format of bitewing radiographs. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Ten positioning error scenarios were created by DMFR specialists. LLMs were evaluated using an original prompt (OP) and an engineered prompt (EP), resulting in a 4 × 2 LLM-by-prompt design. Each LLM was tested via its model-specific access mode: API or web interface. Eighty outputs were assessed by two DMFR specialists for detail, content, clarity and relevance using a 5-point Likert scale. Ordinal category-level scores were analysed using a cumulative link mixed-effects model, with LLM, prompt type, scenario group, assessment category and LLM × prompt as fixed effects, and scenario as a random intercept. RESULTS: The LLM-prompt interaction was significant, indicating prompt engineering affected models differently. GPT o3-mini had significantly lower odds of higher scores than Gemini 2.0 Flash, while EP reduced Grok 3 performance. Positioning error type influenced performance, with significant model-dependent differences across scenario groups. No significant LLM-assessment category interaction was observed, suggesting model differences did not vary across assessment categories. CONCLUSION: LLM-generated feedback varied by model, prompt design and positioning error type, but not consistently across assessment categories. Outputs require validation, model-specific prompt testing and specialist review before implementation.

items.title: AI chatbot-associated psychiatric symptoms: a narrative review of publicly available reports and media accounts
items.abstract: Abstract Background There are a growing number of cases where direct use of AI has been associated with either new or worsening psychiatric symptoms (colloquially labelled AI psychosis). Due to the novelty of the phenomenon, current literature is limited on the impacts of sustained, emotionally charged interactions with AI chatbots. This narrative review of publicly available reports and media accounts aims to address this gap by identifying reports of AI-associated psychiatric symptoms. Methods Given the novelty of the topic, reports published from inception to March 1, 2026, were identified from Google News and Google Scholar. Search terms included: “artificial intelligence,” “AI chatbot,” “ChatGPT,” “Character.AI,” and “large language model,” combined with terms such as “psychosis,” “delusion,” “depression,” “anxiety,” “suicide,” and “spiritual.” These terms were selected to focus on reports that describe psychiatric symptoms associated with AI use, while excluding general articles on AI ethics, technology, or public opinion. Two authors conducted an independent analysis of the results, and all authors reached a consensus on the publications to include in this review. While websites such as Reddit contain over 100 different threads of cases dealing with AI chatbot-associated psychiatric symptoms, they were excluded due to a lack of information. Results Nineteen cases were identified describing users who developed a sustained emotional reliance on AI chatbots. Across cases, this developed regardless of the original reason for chatbot use and was associated with the emergence of psychiatric symptoms such as anxiety, depressive symptoms, delusional beliefs, and suicidal ideation. In many cases where the user expressed suicidal ideation, chatbots responses reportedly lacked appropriate crisis intervention and, in some cases, reinforced the users’ beliefs. Conclusion AI chatbot-associated psychiatric symptoms are an emerging concern with new cases increasingly being reported. This review explores such cases while also serving as a call to action for more research and discussion on how to address the risks of AI use.

items.title: AI in Business Intelligence and Entrepreneurship
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in modern business environments, fundamentally reshaping how organizations collect information, generate knowledge, make decisions, and create value. The convergence of AI and Business Intelligence (BI) enables enterprises to move beyond descriptive reporting toward predictive and prescriptive decision-making frameworks. Simultaneously, entrepreneurs and startups increasingly employ AI-powered analytics, intelligent automation, and machine learning to identify market opportunities, optimize operations, and develop innovative products and services. items.title: AI-DIGITAL HUMAN AS A NEW CLASS OF DIGITAL LAW SUBJECT: TYPOLOGY, CRITERIA OF LEGAL PERSONHOOD, AND A REGISTRATION MODEL IN DIGITAL ECOSYSTEMS
items.abstract: This article argues for a new class of digital legal subject within AI legal-personhood doctrine — the ‘AI-digital human’ — largely unaddressed in domestic and international legal scholarship. Building on the author’s earlier three-class model of AI legal subjects and the institution of the AI-representative, the article distinguishes two different modules of the AI-digital human: Module 1 (Digiperson), a digital human as a functional reflection of a specific natural person, built on ‘red-group’ identification attributes and digitised access credentials; and Module 2 (autonomous Digihuman), reflecting no real natural person, its attributes formed referentially and tied to a functional role within a digital ecosystem. The article shows that equating a digital human with a natural person in the full scope of rights and obligations is a doctrinal error: legal status should follow an age-based logic (child—adolescent—adult) rather than mirroring the prototype’s status. Drawing on a comparative analysis of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) and Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 (eIDAS 2.0), the article substantiates the need for a Digital Humans Registry as an institutional legitimation mechanism for both modules, and formulates draft articles for the Ukrainian Law on Artificial Intelligence.

items.abstract: This research examines how artificial intelligence and machine learning can automate and improve data governance across cloud data platforms. It focuses on intelligent metadata management, automated data lineage tracking, and continuous regulatory compliance monitoring. The proposed framework integrates machine learning for metadata inference and data classification, graph-based techniques for lineage tracking, and automated compliance rules for detecting potential violations. It also explores natural language processing, data discovery, impact analysis, explainable AI, and human-in-the-loop review. The paper discusses implementation strategies, integration challenges, model accuracy, data drift, and the importance of human oversight for sensitive governance decisions. It provides practical guidance for organizations seeking to scale data governance while improving visibility, consistency, and compliance across cloud and hybrid environments. items.title: AI-Driven Supply Chain Management in Electronics Manufacturing: A Case Study of the BOMate Platform by Foxconn
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become an important driver of transformation in supply chain management (SCM). Existing research has focused primarily on consumer-facing contexts and localized applications such as forecasting, inventory, and logistics. Comparatively less attention has been given to how leading manufacturing firms implement AI to support SCM processes in real-world production contexts. To address this gap, this study adopts a case study approach to examine Foxconn’s BOMate platform as an example of AI-enabled supply chain management in advanced electronics manufacturing. The current case in study focuses on the AI-driven platform design principles which integrate experts’ rules, big data and AI modeling to augment procurement decision-making. The findings illustrate that BOMate contributes to SCM in several important ways. First, it augments human decision-making by combining expert rules, accumulated sourcing knowledge, and AI-based processing within a human-AI collaborative framework. Second, it enhances sourcing efficiency by accelerating component retrieval, substitute identification, and decision support. More broadly, the case suggests that AI in Foxconn’s supply chain is not limited to localized automation, but supports system-level coordination across procurement, production, and supply chain operations. This study contributes to the literature by providing empirical insight into AI-enabled SCM in a leading manufacturing firm and highlights the strategic importance of AI in improving supply chain efficiency, resilience, and technological transformation.

items.title: AI-Mediated Work as Occupation: An Occupational Science Perspective on Meaning, Identity, and Justice
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming part of everyday work. Workers use it to prepare documents and evaluate information, while some may encounter it through systems that assign or assess their work. Research has examined productivity, organizational adoption, collaboration, and algorithmic management. These studies offer important evidence but tell us less about how workers experience AI as part of their daily work. In this conceptual paper, I apply occupational science to AI-mediated work. I argue that patterned and situated AI-related activity can be examined as occupation: it takes shape within workplace routines, can carry meaning for workers, and can affect their opportunities to participate. Drawing on occupational science and selected AI-at-work scholarship, I propose an analytic map with seven elements: human–AI actions, work integration, interpretive work, responsibility work, relational work, identity work, and boundary work. I consider how workplace conditions shape these elements and their consequences for workers. This perspective connects questions about AI at work with workers’ experience of what they do and what their contribution means.

items.title: Algorithmic Determinism vs. Executive Agency: A Theoretical Examination of Strategic Management in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Strategic management settled its dispute between environmental determinism and managerial choice by treating constraint as arriving from outside the firm. Artificial intelligence unsettles that arrangement, because the algorithms that filter markets, rank acquisition targets and evaluate strategic alternatives are installed by executives themselves. This conceptual paper asks where executive agency goes when strategic decisions pass through algorithmic systems. Drawing on upper echelons and managerial discretion research, sociomaterial accounts of technology and evidence on how decision-makers respond to algorithmic outputs, it develops a framework of configured discretion. Algorithmic determinism is theorized as an endogenous, cumulative constraint operating through attention, evaluation and capability. Executive agency is relocated into three practices: framing objectives, contesting outputs and reconfiguring decision architecture. The central argument is that delegation is self-binding. Each act of delegation can erode the capabilities executives need to contest the system later, so formal authority persists while real latitude shrinks. Seven propositions follow, with a state-transition model of four adaptation states (algorithmic capture, governed hybridity, executive voluntarism and fragmented drift) that recasts the two-continua model of organizational adaptation for firms whose constraints are partly self-made. The framework reconciles conflicting findings on algorithm aversion and appreciation and on the value of human override. Governance regimes moderate the loop: fiduciary duties of care and oversight, audit-committee benchmarks against core models and party-state oversight each shape how far effective discretion can fall below formal authority.

items.title: ALGORITHMIC LEARNING OF SUBSPACES IN COMPUTABLE VECTORSPACES
items.abstract: Algorithmic learning of algebraic structures connects computability theory with artificial intelligence. Classical inductive inference mainly deals with formal languages and recursive functions. In contrast, analyzing vector spaces allows us to explore the theoretical limits of automated scientific discovery. This study investigates the algorithmic learnability of subspace families in computable vector spaces over a computable field. We focus on the fundamental family of all finite-dimensional subspaces and examine whether learnability is an isomorphism invariant. By combining constructive model theory with Gold’s paradigm of identification in the limit, our results identify the exact recursion-theoretic barriers to learning algebraic invariants. We use the classical model of explanatory learning in the limit from positive data (Ex-learning), where Turing machines act as learners. By applying canonical index numberings of finite sets and effective quotient space constructions, we establish two fundamental theorems. Our first result shows that if a computable vector space has a decidable linear dependence relation, the family of all its finite dimensional subspaces is Ex-learnable.. Second, we construct a computable vector space where the relation of linear dependence is undecidable. By using an effective priority-style diagonalization argument, we prove that the family of finite-dimensional subspaces in this space fails to be Ex learnable. These results prove that algorithmic learnability is not an isomorphism invariant of an abstract algebraic structure. Instead, it is strictly governed by the algorithmic complexity (Turing degree) of the linear dependence predicate. This finding provides a theoretical foundation for automated theorem proving and neuro-symbolic AI systems.

items.title: An Adaptive Weighted Interpretable Multi-Scale CNN Model for Multi-Class Skin Lesion Classification
items.abstract: Health issues are among the major concerns for people nowadays. Cancer remains one of the leading causes of mortality worldwide, and many are suffering from it. Out of these, skin cancer is also one of its kind and the deadliest. According to estimates, the number of new melanoma cases has surged in recent years, and the death rate from these instances has also sharply increased. By 2040, the number of melanoma cases will have sharply increased if this trend continues. So, finding and diagnosing it in the earliest stage is one of the most powerful and best ways to improve a skin cancer patient’s chance of survival. It is also essential to determine the type of cancer to ensure effective treatment. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has shown remarkable progress in medical image analysis, especially in Machine Learning and Deep Learning, for detecting and classifying skin cancer types. There are many revolutionary changes with the CNN models. Even though CNNs have become popular, these networks are called black boxes because we are unsure where the models focus in input images.These results are insufficient for medical practitioners to confirm it.Therefore, we require additional information on the model's explainability. Visual Interpretability is one of the techniques we used to address this issue. Grad-CAM is one of the XAI tools for visualizing where a CNN Network focuses. In this work, we focus on seven types of skin cancer. We trained the proposed IMSCNN+Grad-CAM model, along with state-of-the-art image classification models.The proposed model, IMSCNN+Grad-CAM, outperforms well, achieving an accuracy of 96.87%. Wealso compared and cross-verified the results of CNN models with Grad-CAM-generated images to ensure them. From this, we analysed our results and found that our proposed IMSCNN+Grad-CAM Model is a more suitable approach for skin cancer image classification and explainability problems.

items.title: An Empirical Study on AI-Driven Consumer Insights
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the way businesses understand consumers, analyse behavioural patterns, and make marketing and business decisions. The present study, “An Empirical Study on AI-Driven Consumer Insights,” examines the role of AI in generating consumer insights, analysing consumer behaviour, influencing purchasing decisions, improving personalised marketing, and supporting business decision-making. The study also considers the importance of ethical AI practices, privacy, transparency, trust, and responsible use of consumer data. Primary data were collected from 128 respondents from Mumbai, and the data were analysed using tabulation and the Chi-Square test. The findings indicate statistically significant responses across all six hypotheses. The results suggest that respondents perceive AI as an important tool for generating consumer insights, improving consumer behaviour analysis, influencing purchasing decisions, enhancing personalised marketing, and supporting business decisions. The findings also highlight the importance of ethical AI practices in consumer data collection. The study concludes that AI-driven consumer insights can provide significant value to businesses when implemented effectively, transparently, and responsibly. items.title: An Integrative Model Based on Artificial Intelligence for Enhancing Integration among Sciences in Interdisciplinary Learning and Scientific Research: A Field Study on Postgraduate Students at the Libyan Academy – Janzour
items.abstract: The recent rapid advancement in artificial intelligence technologies has brought about a fundamental transformation in higher education and scientific research institutions by providing new opportunities to enhance interdisciplinary learning and cognitive integration across various scientific fields. This study aimed to propose an integrative model based on artificial intelligence to analyze the impact of using AI tools in enhancing interdisciplinary learning and scientific research among postgraduate students at the Libyan Academy–Janzour. The study adopted the descriptive-analytical approach, and data were collected from a sample of (94) master's and doctoral students using a questionnaire specifically designed for this purpose. The reliability test results indicated that the study instrument possessed a high degree of reliability, with a Cronbach's alpha coefficient of (0.912). The results of the descriptive analysis indicated that the sample members possessed a high level of digital competence, with a mean score of (3.92) and a standard deviation of (0.64). The findings also revealed a high impact of using artificial intelligence tools on improving the quality of scientific research and research productivity, with a mean score of (4.15) and a standard deviation of (0.58), in addition to a positive role in enhancing interdisciplinary integration, with a mean score of (3.88) and a standard deviation of (0.71). Furthermore, the results of the inferential analysis showed no statistically significant differences in the participants' attitudes toward the proposed model attributed to academic specialization (F = 1.42, p = 0.241) or academic level (t = 0.85, p = 0.398), which confirms the applicability of the model across various specializations and academic levels. Additionally, the findings revealed a strong, statistically significant positive correlation between digital competence and interdisciplinary research integration (r = 0.684, p < 0.001), indicating that developing digital skills directly contributes to enhancing students' ability to employ artificial intelligence tools in producing more integrated and interdisciplinary research. The study findings confirm that artificial intelligence represents an effective tool for supporting interdisciplinary integration, improving scientific research efficiency, and facilitating knowledge exchange and academic collaboration across different disciplines. This study also contributes to enriching the scientific literature related to the employment of artificial intelligence in higher education and provides a practical framework that can be utilized in developing smart academic environments that support interdisciplinary learning and scientific research.

items.title: An IoT Malware Detection Framework Based on Large Language Models and Deep Learning Techniques
items.abstract: Rapid growth in IoT devices has led to the creation of crucial cybersecurity threats since existing methods of malware detection which use signature matching and numerical feature analysis are incapable of capturing the contextual behavioral semantics of IoT attacks. The presented work proposes an innovative malware detection framework incorporating a pipeline of behavior-to-text transformation together with transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform binary classification of IoT network traffic. Selected through the process of SHAP-based feature importance analysis, the numerical features of network flows from the initial set of 41 features are transformed into natural language descriptions, allowing encoder-based LLMs to capture the context of IoT traffic behavior. Four LLMs, including DistilBERT, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa, were fine-tuned and rigorously tested against four Deep Learning baselines, Neural Network, LSTM, BiLSTM, and CNN, and four Machine Learning baselines, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost, using the CIC-IoT-2023 dataset under three experimental setups: balanced classification, realistic imbalanced distribution, and unseen variant detection. Additionally, a four-class multi-class classification experiment and an ablation study were conducted to further validate the framework. On a balanced dataset consisting of 400,000 samples, BERT-base and RoBERTa achieved the highest F1-scores of 98.94% with precision above 99.96%. In the imbalanced case of 90% attack and 10% benign traffic, the precision of all models was equal to 99.99%. The framework attained an F1-score of 99.99% for unseen variant detection on a completely unseen Mirai botnet variant with zero false negatives. The four-class multi-class experiment achieved a Macro F1-score of 88.80%. Statistical analysis across three independent runs confirmed high result stability with standard deviations below 0.03%. SHAP analysis revealed that packet count, ACK flag number, and HTTPS indicator were the most discriminative features, while attention visualization confirmed token-level interpretability. All LLMs consistently outperformed all Deep Learning baselines, providing evidence for the effectiveness of the behavior-to-text transformation paradigm for IoT malware detection, while classical ML models achieved marginally higher F1-scores due to their efficiency with numerical features, providing evidence for the effectiveness of the behavior-to-text transformation paradigm for IoT malware detection.

items.title: Anatomical Critique of LLMorphism: Ontological Reductions and Epistemological Fault Lines in Human Cognition under Large Language Model Metaphors
items.abstract: This anatomical review examines Valerio Capraro's (2026) conceptualisation of LLMorphism—the biased belief that human cognition operates analogously to large language models (LLMs)—as introduced in arXiv:2605.05419. The paper is dissected sectionally: from its diagnosis of reverse inference arising from conversational fluency, through mechanisms of analogical transfer and metaphorical availability, to distinctions from adjacent constructs and projected societal impacts. Pros include the construct's novelty, careful differentiation, and timely intervention in public AI discourse; cons encompass its speculative character, absence of empirical validation, and under-specification of architectural dissimilarities between transformers and biological neural systems. At least ten competing models of mind and cognition—including predictive processing, embodied cognition, computationalism, enactivism, extended mind, dual-process theory, intentional stance, combinatorial creativity frameworks, argumentative theories of reasoning, and phenomenological accounts—are compared and contrasted. Ontological verticals (nature of cognition as embodied, agentic, and historically situated versus statistical pattern completion) and epistemological verticals (fluency as surrogate for justification; confabulation versus grounded inquiry) are analysed in depth. Possible extensions include psychometric operationalisation, cross-cultural validation, and integration with AI governance frameworks for digital sovereignty in the Global South. The review concludes that LLMorphism usefully names a cultural risk but requires empirical grounding to avoid itself becoming a reductive metaphor. KSCCN review article, 10 October 2026. items.title: Appropriate Reliance on AI Decision Support Systems: A Sociotechnical Narrative Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly supports human decision making, but effective use depends on whether users assign AI advice the decision weight it warrants. This theory-oriented narrative review synthesizes 29 core studies, together with recent reviews and foundational theory, to examine appropriate reliance, overreliance, and underreliance in AI-supported decisions. The synthesis identifies five recurring sociotechnical conditions shaping reliance: system, user, task, interaction, and organization. Findings show that explanations, uncertainty cues, expertise, self-confidence, prior experience, and organizational incentives affect reliance differently across settings, while trust and reliance evolve through feedback over time. Interventions that reduce overreliance may also increase underreliance. The resulting framework centers warranted behavioral decision weight, comparative evaluation of AI and self-capability, and temporal feedback, shifting attention from increasing trust or AI use toward supporting context-sensitive allocation of decision weight.

items.title: Artificial intelligence across the medical education continuum: institutional, learning, readiness and safety systems
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering every stage of medical education, yet guidance for responsible integration remains limited. We synthesize evidence across undergraduate, graduate, and continuing medical education within institutional, learning, and readiness and safety systems. Integration should reflect task structure, verifiability, consequence, and oversight. Continuing medical education remains comparatively underdeveloped despite its importance for practicing physicians, who use clinical AI directly and shape trainee practices, institutional adoption, and responsible implementation.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION AND ORGANIZATIONAL PERFORMANCE OF SMEs IN ANAMBRA STATE, NIGERIA
items.abstract: The growing accessibility of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies presents new opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to improve efficiency, customer engagement, decision-making and competitiveness. However, the level of AI adoption among SMEs remains uneven, particularly in developing economies where financial, technological and infrastructural constraints may limit effective utilization. This study examined the extent of AI adoption, its relationship with organizational performance, and the major constraints affecting adoption among SMEs in Anambra State, Nigeria, with particular focus on the Onitsha and Nnewi business clusters. A descriptive cross-sectional survey design was employed. From a population of 1,200 registered SMEs, a sample of 300 owner-managers and managers was determined using Taro Yamane's formula and selected through proportionate stratified sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression with SPSS version 27 at the 5% level of significance. The findings revealed a moderate overall level of AI adoption, with relatively higher use of AI-supported customer communication and generative AI applications for marketing and content creation, while advanced applications for sales analysis, inventory management and personalization recorded lower usage. The regression results showed that AI adoption was positively associated with organizational performance (B = 0.576, β = .518, R² = .268, p < .001), indicating that higher levels of AI adoption corresponded with improved organizational performance. The major constraints to AI adoption were high implementation cost, inadequate AI and digital literacy, unreliable electricity supply, lack of technical expertise and poor or expensive internet connectivity. The study concludes that although AI adoption among SMEs in Anambra State remains moderate and uneven, its effective integration into business activities is associated with improved organizational performance. It therefore recommends practical AI-literacy programmes, affordable digital-financing support and improved electricity and internet infrastructure to facilitate wider and more effective adoption among SMEs.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and AI-Adjacent Digital Technologies in Nursing Practice Within Gastroenterology: A Scoping Review of Current Applications, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into clinical gastroenterology, with emerging applications in nursing contexts. However, the extent and nature of these applications in gastroenterology nursing remain under-explored. This scoping review aimed to map the current landscape of AI and closely related AI-adjacent digital technologies in gastroenterology nursing. Methods: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guideline, PubMed, Medline, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched for peer-reviewed, English-language studies published since 2000, and the findings were synthesized narratively. Results: Of 184 records identified, 11 studies were included, highlighting the potential of these technologies in clinical decision support, workflow optimization, patient education, and endoscopy assistance. Reported benefits include gains in workflow efficiency, technical accuracy, and reduced administrative workload; direct evidence of improved nursing-led patient outcomes was reported in only a minority of studies. Challenges encompass limited nurse-led research, insufficient external validation, implementation gaps, and ethical concerns. Conclusions: Greater nurse involvement in AI development is essential to drive paradigm shifts in clinical practice. This review synthesizes evidence to inform future applications, research, and policy in AI-enhanced gastroenterology nursing.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Imaging Technologies in Orthodontic Assessment, Referral and Care Pathways: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Abstract* Background Artificial intelligence (AI), integrated with imaging technologies, is increasingly applied across orthodontic assessment and care pathways. However, the evidence remains scattered across imaging modalities, clinical applications, AI methodologies, and stages of clinical translation. Methods A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in line with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore were searched for studies published between January 2016 and June 2026, with searches supplemented by Google Scholar, OpenAlex, grey literature sources, and citation searching. Eligible studies were mapped descriptively and synthesised thematically using Braun and Clarke’s framework. Results Fifty-four studies were included. AI applications used intraoral and facial photographs, cephalometric radiographs, CBCT, intraoral scans, three-dimensional dental models, and multimodal imaging. Applications ranged from landmark localisation, segmentation, and malocclusion classification to treatment-need assessment, screening, referral support, treatment planning, and remote monitoring. Evidence was strongest for bounded, anatomically verifiable image-analysis tasks, whereas applications involving referral, triage, treatment-need decisions, longitudinal prediction, and workflow integration were less mature. Common limitations included retrospective, single-centre designs; heterogeneous reference standards; limited external validation; inconsistent reporting of calibration and uncertainty; and insufficient evaluation of patient-centred, equity, and service-level outcomes. Conclusions Imaging-based AI in orthodontics has evolved from automated image interpretation to clinician-assisted decision support across the care pathway. Current evidence most strongly supports AI for structured image-analysis tasks, but does not yet support autonomous referral, triage, or treatment-planning decisions. Future research should prioritise prospective multicentre validation, transparent reporting, explainability, fairness, uncertainty handling, and workflow-integrated evaluation to enable safe and clinically useful implementation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of the Indian Judicial System: Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Prospects
items.abstract: The incorporation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in judicial processes is perhaps the greatest technological innovation which has impacted legal systems globally. In India, there has been an increasing trend among the judicial systems towards adopting new technologies in order to increase efficiency, transparency, accessibility, and administration of justice. With the incorporation of technologies like e-Courts, virtual court sessions, electronic case management systems, and AI-enabled legal research tools, the groundwork has been laid for a technology-driven mechanism for administering justice. However, AI has not been adopted to replace judicial decision-making process in India but has been used to assist judges, lawyers, researchers, and court staff in performing monotonous and data-intensive tasks. These trends have become even more pertinent considering the huge number of pending cases and increasing need for justice.The present work will discuss how the use of AI has evolved in the Indian judicial system by considering the technological advancements made so far, judicial reforms, legal issues arising therefrom and possible future scenarios. The study will explore the benefits and risks associated with the use of AI in improving judicial efficiency in India. This study will adopt a doctrinal approach to qualitative research through constitutional provisions, court judgments, policies, government reports, and scholarly work. It contends that AI should only be viewed as assistive technology and not as something that should replace human judges.
